Q: Visual Studio 2026 and Windows 10 compatibility A:

All Windows SDK versions have supported targeting multiple Windows versions.

API surface is controlled by macro (WINVER and/or _WIN32_WINNT), see Update WINVER and _WIN32_WINNT and Using the Windows Headers: Setting WINVER or _WIN32_WINNT

When you use the Windows SDK, you can specify which versions of Windows your code can run on. The preprocessor macros WINVER and _WIN32_WINNT specify the minimum operating system version your code supports. Visual Studio and the Microsoft C++ compiler support targeting Windows 7 SP1 and later. Older build tools include support for Windows XP SP2, Windows Server 2003 SP1, Vista, and Windows Server 2008. Windows 95, Windows 98, Windows ME, Windows NT, and Windows 2000 are unsupported.

Sometimes you also need the /SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS,x.y argument to LINK.exe or EDITBIN.exe, for example /SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS,5.1 was needed to run on Windows XP (as well as a different C++ runtime import library). But you only need to do this when targeting OS versions that are no longer officially supported, because the default value here is the oldest supported version.

Q: External USB Fingerprint scanner A:

So this might not be possible on iOS as the OS treats fingerprints as highly sensitive biometric data since apps never get the fingerprint image or template. I think at most, your technical solution can only solve for "does this fingerprint match one already enrolled on the device?".

In terms of React Native and Expo limitations: they both have biometric APIs (expo-local-authentication, react-native-fingerprint-scanner, etc..) but from the ones I found, they seem to only support authentication, not enrollment or capture which would only work with the device's built-in biometric hardware.

With regard to the the USB biometric device you mentioned, this would likely only work on Android and you would need a vendor-specific native SDK from the biometric device.

You might be able to look into https://github.com/biometric-technologies/biometric-sdk which may support what you're looking to do, it's written in Kotlin and it could be a useful example as I don't know much about the SDK itself; it doesn't seem like the contributors still maintain it but reading some of the code could help you gauge their technical solution and see how it could be applied for yours.

Q: SQLite.Interop.dll missing after publishing a Windows Forms .NET application A:

This is a common fix, especially when using NuGet packages:

  1. In Solution Explorer, right-click your project and select Add > New Folder. Name it x64.

  2. Repeat the process to create an x86 folder.

  3. Right-click the new x64 folder > Add > Existing Item.

  4. Browse to your project's bin or debug folder (the exact location might vary by your project type and NuGet version, but common paths include bin/x64 or runtimes/win-x64/native). Select the SQLite.Interop.dll file and click OK.

  5. Repeat step 4 for the x86 folder and its corresponding DLL.

  6. For both DLL files you just added to the solution (inside the new x64 and x86 folders), right-click the file, select Properties, and change the Copy to Output Directory option to Copy always.

Q: How to quickly test database access via a connection string A:

You haven't mentioned what database you are connecting to, however. In SQL Server 2005, from .NET, you can specify a connection timeout in your connection string like so:

server=<server>;database=<database>;uid=<user>;password=<password>;Connect Timeout=3

This will try to connect to the server and if it doesn't do so in three seconds, it will throw a timeout error.

Q: Error CS9293: Cannot use an extension parameter in this context A:

The error occurs because extension parameters can only be used inside non‑static methods of the extension block. Static methods don't capture the extension parameter, so the compiler reports CS9293.

To fix it, remove the static modifier:

public int Baz() => bar % 2; // <-- removed 'static'
